newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nobel fund aims to make millionaires of laureates.
newsitem.headline: Nobel fund aims to make millionaires of laureates.

text.p: Sweden's Nobel Foundation has the daunting task of ensuring that there will be sufficient funds in the future to continue providing appropriate financial awards to the winners of Nobel prizes.

This year winners of each prize will receive 7.4 million Swedish crowns, or $1.12 million -- roughly equivalent to the Nobel Prize's value in real terms when the first award of 150,000 crowns was given in 1901.

Alfred Nobel, the Swedish scientist who invented dynamite, stipulated in his will setting up the prizes that most of his estate should be invested in a fund and the income used to reward those who "have conferred the greatest benefit to mankind."

Fund manager Michael Sohlman, grandson of the original executor of Nobel's will, said in a recent interview that investment strategy had strayed somewhat from Nobel's original wishes in order to cope with erosion of the endowment, which collapsed in value by two-thirds in its first 50 years.

"He wanted all his real assets to be sold and put into safe securities and into gilt-edged bonds, which was reasonable at the time, when real interest rates were low or negative," Sohlman said at the foundation's Stockholm headquarters.
"Our target now is to keep the prize unchanged in real terms," added Sohlman.

It was not until 1991 that the fund's value was recovered, thanks to its previous manager, Baron Stig Ramel, who was one of the few investors to steer clear of Sweden's real estate crash of the early 1990s.
In that year the foundation raised the value of the award by 50 percent to 6 million crowns (now about $897,000).

Sohlman said the fund, which owns exclusive real estate in central Stockholm and the Norwegian Nobel Institute in Oslo, had the responsibility to ensure the Nobel prizes would exist well beyond the next century.
"We've been in business for 100 years, so 50 years is not on our planning horizon. Our intention is, of course, to go on forever," he said.

"Through diversification we have managed to increase the share of equities but decrease the overall risk. So overall the risk of the portfolio is at the same level as if we had only fixed income," Sohlman said.
The fund posted a profit in 1995 of 176 million crowns ($26.7 million) before appropriations, down from 221 million crowns ($33.6 million) in 1994.

Administration costs are high, roughly equal to the amount given away in prize money. This year the foundation will give the institutions that choose winners 42.2 million crowns ($6.4 million) for the costs of assessing the candidates.

"Nobel Week" in December each year, when winners and their families are flown to Sweden or Norway to accept their prizes and attend a gala dinner, cost the foundation 5.7 million crowns ($865,000) last year.
Any calculation error could leave the foundation red-faced in front of the world's best mathematicians and economists.
"We had this deplorable situation in 1992 when the laureates were told they were awarded a prize worth $1.2 million and when they came for it they found a prize worth $950,000," Sohlman said.
The fund, which manages capital worth 2.3 billion crowns ($349 million), realised an 8.3 percent return on assets in 1995.

About 64 percent of the fund's assets are invested in stocks -- 10 percent in Sweden, 16 percent in other European countries, 18 percent in the United States, 9 percent in Japan and 11 percent in emerging markets.
The rest of the fund is invested in equal shares of interest-bearing securities and real estate.
The fund's heavy exposure to Japanese markets last year, where it had 189 million crowns ($28.7 million invested) in Japanese funds, capped profits.

"We have changed the geographical weighting, some of which has been successful and some has not," Sohlman said. "Japan has not produced the result we had expected, but we share this fate with others."
Early critics of the prizes said giving Swedish money away to foreigners was not right, Sohlman said. But Nobel was emphatic on this point.

"No consideration whatever shall be given to the nationality of the candidates, but that the most worthy shall receive the prize, whether he be a Scandinavian or not," Nobel wrote in his will, dated 1895.

Nobel said Swedish institutes should award the literature prize and scientific awards in medicine, physics and chemistry but the Peace Prize would be awarded in Oslo by members of the Norwegian parliament.
At the time of Nobel's death in 1896, Sweden and Norway were united politically, a union which ended in 1905.
The economics prize was first awarded in 1968 by Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, to commemorate its 300th anniversary.
